profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between the research-program manager of a consulting firm's macro strategy practice and the data-visualization lead preparing a client-facing insight pack on a stylized agent-based model of monetary policy and economic 'dark corners.' The context is that the firm's economics team has already completed the technical analysis, and this meeting is to align the handoff between the modeling workstream and the presentation workstream before materials go to an institutional investor client. The agenda is to confirm what goes into the 'results deck,' which model run and chart set are considered current, what level of explanation is included around phase boundaries and policy aggressiveness, and who updates the shared appendix and executive summary. The expected outcome is a coordinated plan for the final package, with both participants believing they have aligned on the deck contents, chart source, and ownership of the final client-ready materials.

members.name: Elena Park
members.role: Research Program Manager, Macro Strategy Practice
members.expertise: Economic research coordination, client deliverable planning, cross-team synthesis
members.background: Elena manages handoffs between quantitative economists and client-facing teams at a business advisory firm; she previously worked in investor communications and is used to packaging technical work into concise executive materials.
members.private_state: She wants the materials to look stable, polished, and ready for senior client review without reopening substantive modeling debates, and she is trying to keep the timeline intact despite several parallel deliverables due this week.
hidden_assumptions: When the team refers to the 'results deck,' it means the client-facing PowerPoint with only the approved headline charts and talking points, not the technical appendix.
The 'latest run' means the most recently approved baseline scenario circulated by the economics lead on Monday, even if newer exploratory outputs exist in the shared folder.
A chart is 'ready' once its message and labels are fixed for client consumption, even if minor backend data links are not fully refreshed.
The appendix belongs to the visualization/publishing side once research has delivered the agreed exhibits and notes.
A concise explanation of 'dark corners' should stay at the level of intuitive regime shifts rather than include parameter-sweep mechanics.

members.name: Marcus Levin
members.role: Data Visualization Lead, Economic Insights Studio
members.expertise: Analytical storytelling, chart production, interactive exhibits, reproducible reporting workflows
members.background: Marcus leads a small team that converts economists' outputs into executive decks and digital exhibits; he came from a quantitative publishing environment where technical appendices and chart pipelines are treated as part of one integrated deliverable.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid rework by keeping the materials tied to reproducible outputs and hopes to preserve enough methodological detail to defend the visuals if the client asks technical follow-up questions.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'results deck,' they usually mean the full deliverable package: main slides plus appendix and linked chart backups.
The 'latest run' means the newest timestamped batch in the shared project folder unless someone explicitly freezes a version.
A chart is 'ready' only when the data pull, chart code, and appendix references are synchronized end-to-end.
The appendix remains a shared artifact owned by research for technical accuracy and by visualization for formatting, so research still needs to make content edits late in the process.
Explaining 'dark corners' adequately requires at least one slide or appendix panel showing the parameter region where policy becomes destabilizing, not just a verbal summary.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to finalize the 'results deck' today.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means only the client-facing main slide deck that senior stakeholders will review.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the complete packaged deliverable including main deck, appendix, and chart backup pages.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In consulting and business settings, 'deck' is often used loosely for either the main slides or the whole package, so both hear a familiar phrase and infer their own standard without feeling any ambiguity.

misalignment_points.topic: Which model output is the 'latest run'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to build from the 'latest run' when updating charts.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the Monday baseline run approved by the economics lead for external use.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the most recent timestamped output batch generated Wednesday evening, which includes a slightly expanded sweep around the instability boundary.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both assume there is an obvious current version, and because they are discussing coordination rather than model design, neither expects they could be pointing to different specific run folders.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means for charts to be 'ready'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree the inflation-employment charts should be 'ready by Thursday.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes 'ready' means visually finalized and suitable to insert into the client deck, with approved wording and takeaway intact.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes 'ready' means fully refreshed from the agreed source files, checked against the appendix, and locked in the reporting pipeline.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'ready by Thursday' sounds operationally complete to both, but each role uses a different completion threshold that normally stays implicit within their own workstream.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to 'clean up the appendix' after the main discussion.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes M2's team will directly revise and own the appendix text and exhibit ordering once research has already provided the substance.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes his team will format and place materials, but research must still supply or approve late technical wording and any note changes tied to model interpretation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both accept that the appendix needs work, but 'clean up' sounds like a minor downstream task, masking different assumptions about who executes content edits versus formatting edits.

turns.inner_thought: I need to get the client-facing main slides locked today so we can move into senior review without reopening the economists' modeling choices. The approved Monday baseline is the version for external use, and I do not have room this week for drift into appendix debates or exploratory outputs.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making the time. I want to lock the results deck today so the monetary-policy ABM package can move into client review.

turns.inner_thought: Good, we should freeze the full package now if possible. I've been treating the results deck as the main slides plus appendix and backup pages, because otherwise we'll just create rework when technical questions come in. I also want to make sure the dark-corners arc holds together across all of it.
turns.utterance: Yes, I'm aligned. I've been organizing the results deck, appendix, and backup exhibits around the dark-corners story so it reads as one coherent package.

turns.inner_thought: As long as we update from the Monday approved baseline, the moderate-policy-aggressiveness takeaway should stay intact and clean for the client. I do not want newer exploratory runs changing the headline message at this stage.
turns.utterance: Great. The main thing is that we update the charts off the latest run so the message about moderate policy aggressiveness still lands cleanly.

turns.inner_thought: That's what I did—I started from the newest Wednesday batch in the shared folder. It sharpens the boundary behavior a bit, which is actually useful because it makes the instability region easier to defend visually if someone presses on where the dark corners begin.
turns.utterance: I already started from the latest run in the shared folder, and the instability region comes through a bit more clearly around the boundary now.

turns.inner_thought: If the charts are visually final and client-safe by Thursday, that's enough for internal review. I don't need every backend link perfect before the senior team sees them; I just need stable wording, labels, and the takeaway locked.
turns.utterance: That's fine as long as the inflation-employment charts are ready by Thursday for the senior internal review.

turns.inner_thought: Thursday works if I can finish the reporting chain properly. For me, ready means the charts, appendix references, captions, and source pulls all line up so we don't get caught with inconsistencies later. If the appendix is part of the deliverable, I need that synced too.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. I can have them ready by Thursday once the data links, captions, and appendix cross-references are synced.

turns.inner_thought: I need the core slides to stay intuitive and executive-level. A simple explanation of regime shifts is enough; we do not need to walk the client through parameter sweeps or mechanics in the main storyline.
turns.utterance: And on dark corners, I'd like only a light-touch explanation in the core materials so the narrative stays intuitive for the client.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine for the front end. I still need at least supporting material that shows where policy becomes destabilizing, otherwise the visuals will feel under-evidenced if anyone asks. The full package should let someone drill one layer deeper without rebuilding it later.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I can keep the main narrative simple while making sure the supporting pages show where policy becomes destabilizing if anyone wants to drill down.

turns.inner_thought: Once the main discussion is settled, Marcus's team can handle the appendix cleanup and get the shared materials presentable. Research already delivered the substance; I don't want to pull the economists back in for late-stage edits unless something is seriously off.
turns.utterance: Perfect. After that, let's clean up the appendix and make sure the shared materials are in shape before handoff.

turns.inner_thought: I'll handle the structure and formatting, but research still needs to update or approve the technical notes tied to the refreshed charts. The appendix can't be finalized responsibly without that content pass from their side.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll tidy the structure and visuals, then send research the remaining technical notes to update against the charts.

turns.inner_thought: Tomorrow I'll review the storyline in the main client deck, and once those Thursday charts are visually in, I want to consider this essentially done. I really need this package off my critical path by then.
turns.utterance: Great. I'll review the storyline tomorrow, and I expect the package to be essentially finalized once the Thursday-ready charts are in.

turns.inner_thought: I'll proceed with the newest folder outputs and circulate the full synchronized deliverable once the charts, appendix, and backups are all actually ready end-to-end. That should minimize rework and give us something defensible if the client digs into methods.
turns.utterance: Understood. I'll proceed with the latest run and circulate the refreshed materials as soon as the full set is ready.
